entries.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
entries.summary: Scant data about serious adverse effects makes it harder to answer scientific and legal questions about how often the drugs might cause serious harm like blindness or pancreatitis.
entries.content:
Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often

Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION, for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.

Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.

His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.

In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.

A partial database

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events. It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.

The legal challenge

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."

NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."

Uncertainty in reporting

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.

He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.

"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."

Calls to poison control

The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.

"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.

These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.

But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed

"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.

NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

entries.title: A year of ceasefire in Gaza through the lens of NPR's reporter
entries.summary: It has been one year since Hamas released the remaining Israeli hostages and President Trump promised an end to the war, but Palestinians say the past 12 months have been a ceasefire in name only.
entries.content:
NPR's Anas Baba captures one year of ceasefire in Gaza : The Picture ShowIt has been one year since Hamas released the remaining Israeli hostages and President Trump promised an end to the war, but Palestinians say the past 12 months have been a ceasefire in name only.

A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.

GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.

A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.

Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.

That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.

NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.

Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

A child's toys are stained with blood in Gaza City on Sept. 1, 2026, following an Israeli operation to kidnap a Hamas security officer. His family was killed in Israeli airstrikes. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Anas Baba/NPR

entries.title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
entries.summary: Democrats are hoping to win back Latino voters who have soured on both parties. They hope Latino content creators will bridge the gap.
entries.content:
After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help

Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.

That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.

This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.

One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.

"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.

That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.

"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.

Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.

BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.

Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.

"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."

Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.

Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.

"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.

In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.

It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.

This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.

Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.

"Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.

Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.

So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.

"Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.

So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.

"My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.

Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.

"The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.

entries.title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
entries.summary: Carve a pumpkin? You can do better than that. Fun and unusual ways to celebrate the season, from writing a gratitude letter to making an ancestral altar.
entries.content:
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.

Life Kit

It's fall. Let's get cozy!

Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.

Eat warming foods

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook, shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup: a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days.

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta.

Make time for introspection

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person?

Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."

If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions.)

Create cozy vibes at home

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste, says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month. "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.

Do something indulgent for yourself

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit, she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."

Create a home theater. Devika Girish, co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine, explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.

Recharge your energy

Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto, likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks, says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity. If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.

Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours.

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta.

Deepen your connections

Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering. Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.

Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari, a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions, shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.

Your turn: What are some creative ways you celebrate the fall season?

Email us at lifekit@npr.org with your response and full name, and we may feature your story on NPR.

This digital story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter.

entries.title: The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)
entries.summary: In a blockbuster show, The Metropolitan Museum of Art places the work of two major 20th century artists side by side: the married couple Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock.
entries.content:
The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)

There's a new blockbuster show at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Past Continuous features two artists: Jackson Pollock, with many of his instantly recognizable "drip" paintings, and Lee Krasner, an artist often overshadowed by Pollock, who was her husband. But in this major exhibition, Krasner is finally getting her due — and on her own terms.

This gargantuan show is replete with Pollock's greatest hits, the giant, frozen dances of paint splashed on canvas that have become iconic. But this exhibition of more than 120 works (74 from Krasner, and 48 from Pollock) reveals Krasner as an Abstract Expressionist titan, too.

One of the first works that catches your eye is a 1955 Krasner collage.

"Collage was very catalytic for her at these crucial moments in her life," said Brinda Kumar, one of the two Met curators who put together this exhibition. "She was literally sometimes tearing up older bodies of work to create a new chapter."

This work is 1955's Bald Eagle, a riotous mix of browns, blacks, fuchsia, and orange, with a claw-like slash of yellow. And right in the middle is a cutout whose shape evokes the head of a bald eagle — and that's the name that Krasner gave to this collage.

Pollock's rejects were the source material for Bald Eagle, according to Kumar. "Krasner has very intentionally and deliberately cut up discarded Pollock works from this era in the 1950s, where you can see his distinctive drip still evident," she said.

When you put Krasner's collages next to Pollock's drip paintings, we see something new in the juxtaposition, said another Met curator, David Breslin.

"But that doesn't mean that the individual parts forgo their histories or their pasts," Breslin said. "We see that almost as a metaphor for couples in relationships as well. You form a unit, yet you also have all the things in your head, in your mind, in your heart that are your own, that don't change."

And sure enough, just past these collages, a visitor will see one of Pollock's classic drip paintings — 1952's Convergence, with neon orange and electric yellow so bright and bold that they foreshadow 1980s subway graffiti. The curators have put Convergence on a freestanding wall near windows, with daylight shining through — evoking the energy of a contemporary gallery.

The unspoken challenge of this show is to invite comparisons between wife-and-husband artists. In popular imagination, Pollock is often the troubled genius and hero, and Krasner is sidelined as a helpmate. She knew what people thought — but she didn't care.

In a 1978 interview on a television program called Inside New York's Art World, the interviewer asked Krasner what she was doing while Pollock was becoming so famous.

"I was working all the time," Krasner replied. "I doubt our relationship could have existed at all if I weren't working. In terms of what other people think, I can't do anything about that. You know, that's not my preoccupation anyway. As long as I was able to work, I went about my business."

That's true, but Krasner was also very savvy about her market value as a female artist, said curator Brinda Kumar.

"She was very cognizant of the gender dynamics and the gender politics. His career was the one that was more successful at the time."

To that end, she made certain calculations. They made their home in Springs, N.Y., a small fishing community on the far side of Long Island — a location Krasner chose specifically to get Pollock away from the business and booze of Manhattan. Pollock used a barn on the property to work on his enormous canvases, while Krasner painted first in the kitchen and then in a small, upstairs bedroom.

Charting her own course

Lee Krasner was all about reinvention — both artistic and personal. Born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn, she was the child of Orthodox Jewish parents who came from a shtetl in what is now Ukraine. Nobody in her family knew anything about art.

She gave herself a series of new names: first Lenore, then Lee Krasner. She sculpted a new life as a young, bold artist. And she became a quintessential networker who knew everybody in New York's art scene.

Journalist Mary Gabriel has written extensively about Krasner, including in her 2018 book Ninth Street Women: Lee Krasner, Elaine de Kooning, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler: Five Painters and the Movement that Changed Modern Art. Gabriel says that unlike her husband, Krasner kept reinventing her style.

"Krasner was so fascinating because she changed, not even by the decade. Every few years, she tries something new," Gabriel said. "She was always searching, which in a way is the most, I think, honest way to be an artist, because art is about discovery."

These include what Krasner called her "Little Images" — densely populated paintings from the late 1940s of nearly hieroglyphic looking symbols, all jostling for space on small canvases — as well as immense works she created, especially after Pollock died in a car crash in 1956. Pollock was plagued by alcoholism and depression, and he cheated on her; his girlfriend of the time was one of the passengers in the crash.

Krasner continued to be financially savvy as well. After Pollock's death, she more than tripled the price of one of his most famous works, Autumn Rhythm (Number 30), to sell it to the Met — a sum that not just set the pace for Pollock's market value, but for a tide of modern artists.

For this show, Autumn Rhythm was moved off its traditional museum wall to a freestanding display, Kumar noted.

"It is almost architectural in a way, because it's set against this slate grey color," she said. "The swirling blacks get animated in a whole new way, and the familiar teals and the familiar whites surge with a new energy."

Krasner seized upon her own new energy in the years after Pollock's death. She took over the barn studio that had been her husband's — and made giant, joyful work, brimming with life and lushness, as curator David Breslin noted.

"You see this incredible painting that's almost 17 feet wide called The Seasons, that has these forms and bodies, eyes and body parts and these things that look like vegetation sprawling out of it," Breslin said. "So she makes, almost in a contradictory way, some of the brightest, most vibrant paintings the year after his death."

And in some way, this whole show is all about Lee Krasner finally being able to claim her own space. Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous runs at the Met until Jan. 31.

entries.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
entries.summary: Indian authorities have launched a major security crackdown in New Delhi, detaining thousands of protesters who intended to hold a mass demonstration against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
entries.content:
India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief

Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.

The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.

Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.

Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.

Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.

"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.

Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"

The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.

"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.

India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.

The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.

The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.

The commission and the government deny the allegations.

India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi

For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

entries.title: Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
entries.summary: The prediction market company says it wants to prevent its platform from being abused by criminals. The company is facing mounting pressure over market manipulation and insider trading on the site.
entries.content:
Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering

Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.

Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement, regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity there. The platform has exploded in growth in the past year.

According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.

In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn after his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.

"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."

The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.

At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.

Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.

Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.

Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.

The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.

During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

entries.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
entries.summary: The three fired workers say OpenAI punished them for being outspoken about safety. The company disputes the claims and says they were fired over mishandling sensitive information.
entries.content:
Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.

OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.

In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.

"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.

In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.

OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.

In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.

"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

entries.title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
entries.summary: Trump says the U.S. will obtain diesel from Russia, relaxing years of U.S. pressure on Moscow, to combat prices before midterms. He said he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.
entries.content:
Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.

Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash

Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."

"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.

The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.

The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.

Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

entries.title: The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
entries.summary: The Pentagon says it will livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan at Fort Hood, the site of his 2009 mass shooting. That would be the first public execution in the U.S. since the 1930s.
entries.content:
The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that

The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II.

The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.

But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.

"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."

If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.

"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was 90 years ago

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.

Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS. People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.

"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.

The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.

He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.

"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."

He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.

In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.

"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."

Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low.

"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."

Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.

"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."

Leaders call for Hegseth to reverse course

Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President Vance told reporters, "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, similarly mused on CNN about whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.

The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."

"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.

Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also called on the Pentagon to revoke its decision, saying, "A country cannot condone livestreaming a man's death for entertainment."

"We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square," she wrote on X. "Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?"
